text: Neighborhood. My old neighborhood was three blocks from the beach.
Block. The bakery is two blocks from my building.
Crosswalk. Wait at the crosswalk, the cars here do not stop.
Doorman. Ask the doorman, he knows everything about this street.
Crowded. The metro is crowded until nine in the morning.
Traffic. There is a lot of traffic on this avenue.
Rush hour. At rush hour it takes forty minutes to go four blocks.
Within walking distance. The park is within walking distance, so I never take the car.
Send me a photo of your street. I want to see where you live now.
Hold on. There are some trees, there's a crosswalk, and that is basically it.
Is it noisy? It looks like a big avenue behind you.
At rush hour there is a lot of traffic. On Sunday there isn't much noise at all.
And your building? Mine has nothing, not even an elevator.
There's a doorman, Jorge, who has been here longer than the building, I think.
Okay, but what is actually near you? Anything good?
Two blocks away there's the place where you buy bread, the bakery, which opens at six.
Six in the morning? Nothing opens at six here. Are there parks?
There aren't much, sorry, there aren't many parks, but one is within walking distance.
That sounds better than you said at the start. Is it crowded on Saturdays?
Very. And I like it, which I did not expect. There is no beach, but there are a hundred other things.
There's a bakery on the corner that opens at five.
Jorge, who has been here for twenty years, is the doorman.
My street, which used to be very quiet, is full of cars now.
The park everybody goes to is within walking distance.
It's the place where you buy bread.

When we moved, it was only four miles, but it felt like another country. On my old street there was a bakery on the corner which opened at five in the morning, and the woman who ran it knew everybody's name. There were children my own age in every building, so I was never inside the house. The new street, which looks nicer in photos, had nothing on the corner at all, and for the first month I thought there was nobody here my age. Then I met a girl walking a dog that never stops barking, and it turned out she lives two floors below me. So the street I hated in March is the one I would not leave now. It did not change. I just met the people who were already in it.

Welcome to the neighborhood walk. The whole route is six blocks and it takes about forty minutes at an easy pace. Start at the square behind you. On this first street you will pass the building with the green door, which is the oldest one here, and a bakery that has been in the same family for three generations. Now, on the second block, look for the crosswalk painted in yellow. The park you can see from there is the one everybody uses at the weekend, though it gets crowded after ten. The last street, which most visitors miss, has the small market where people who live here actually do their shopping. Take your time, and mind the traffic at the corner.
